summary.lead: 412 hectares of drained fen on the lower Havel are returned to wetland hydrology, so that water is held in the catchment through the summer and fen habitat recovers.
summary.what: The site was drained for grassland in the 1960s and the peat has been oxidising since. The works close the drainage ditches, install adjustable weirs and raise the water table in stages between 2027 and 2029, over 412 hectares inside a 1,840 km² catchment.
summary.why: Two results are expected. Water is retained in the catchment and released more slowly through the low-flow months, which matters to abstractors downstream. And fen vegetation and breeding waders recover on ground that is currently too dry for them.
summary.measured: For water: groundwater level, rewetted area and additional low-flow volume retained. For biodiversity: habitat condition, breeding wader pairs and area in favourable condition. Baselines were recorded between 2024 and 2026. Each figure is verified by DEMO Hydro-Verify GmbH against the monitoring plan before any unit is issued.

detail.worksBody: 2027: 14 km of drainage ditch closed and eight adjustable weirs installed. 2028: water level raised to the first target and held. 2029: second raise, then the level is maintained. Mowing is withdrawn from 180 hectares and continues elsewhere to keep the fen open.
detail.baselineBody: Groundwater was logged at six piezometers from spring 2024 to spring 2026, so the baseline covers two full hydrological years including one dry summer. Habitat condition was scored on 24 fixed plots in 2025 and 2026. The baseline report is listed in the documents section.
detail.riskBody: A run of dry years would slow the rise in groundwater and delay the outcome, which is why a buffer is held back in every period. Peat that has already been lost does not return. The project states its uncertainty per metric rather than offering a single confidence figure.

outcomes.lead: What is measured, against what baseline, by what method, and with what stated uncertainty.
outcomes.noCombinedScore: Water and biodiversity are reported separately and are not combined into a single score. They measure unrelated things, and the buyers who fund this work weigh them differently.

groundwater.metric: Mean summer groundwater level below surface

rewetted.method: Water level records and aerial imagery, assessed against the hydrological criteria in the monitoring plan.

lowflow.metric: Additional water retained in the catchment during low flow
lowflow.method: Modelled from measured water levels and site storage capacity, recalculated each year against the gauge record at Rathenow.

condition.method: The scheme's condition assessment on 24 fixed plots, scored by a qualified assessor every second year.

waders.method: Three territory mapping visits per breeding season, following the scheme's survey protocol.

favourable.method: Condition scores mapped to area from the plot network and the vegetation survey.

record.title: Public transaction record
record.lead: Every step of a transaction agreed on this platform is written here as a new entry. Entries are added; they are never edited and never deleted.

scope.title: What this record is, and what it is not
scope.isBody: Evidence of what was agreed on this platform, in the order it happened. Each entry states the project, the type of event, the date it occurred, and the counterparty as that counterparty appears publicly.
scope.isSecond: It is permanent. An entry that has been written stays written and stays readable, including an entry that turned out to be wrong.
scope.isNotBody: It is not the scheme registry. Each credit scheme runs its own official database of issued and retired units and gives outside systems no write access to it. Whether a unit exists, and whether it has been retired, is answered by that registry and not by this page.
scope.isNotSecond: It is not a price list and not a volume report. The record carries no unit volumes and no prices.

how.title: How to read an entry
how.appendOnlyTitle: Nothing is edited and nothing is deleted
how.appendOnlyBody: A mistake is corrected by a new entry that points at the entry it corrects. The corrected entry stays visible, in date order, marked as superseded. A superseded entry is still part of the record.
how.labelBody: A buyer appears as a label such as “Buyer 014”, together with its sector, country and size band. Labels are allocated per project and per deal: the same label on two projects is not the same organisation, and two deals by one organisation on one project carry different labels.
how.disclosureTitle: Being named is the counterparty's choice, deal by deal
how.disclosureBody: Where a counterparty has chosen to be named for a deal, the organisation is named on that deal's entries from the date of that choice onward. Entries published before that date keep the label they were published with, because nothing already published is rewritten.
how.ownerBody: The organisation that owns a project is named on that project's entries. It is already named on the project page, so a label would hide nothing.
how.registryTitle: Registry references belong to the scheme
how.registryBody: An entry recording an allocation, a transfer or a retirement references a record in the scheme's own registry. That reference is what makes the entry checkable. The authoritative record stays with the scheme.

correction.title: How the correction in this extract works
correction.body: One entry in this extract was recorded against the wrong period. The record has no way to change an entry, so it was corrected the only way it can be: by adding entries.
correction.step1: Entry {wrong} recorded the event against the wrong period.
correction.step2: Entry {correction} points at entry {wrong} and states the reason. Entry {wrong} is neither changed nor removed; it is marked as superseded and stays in date order.
correction.step3: Entry {corrected} records the event again, with the period taken from the signed letter of intent.
correction.close: Three entries, all visible. A reader can see what was recorded, that it was wrong, why, and what replaced it.

limits.title: Limits of this extract
limits.privacy: The content of a private deal room is not published: not the messages, not the draft documents, not the terms and not the prices. The record states that an event happened, not what was in it.
limits.kAnonymity: Every row carries a sector, a country and a size band. Where an organisation is named on one deal, those three attributes may still be enough to match it to entries where it appears only as a label. Whether the sector groups and size bands are broad enough to prevent that is an open question for the client, and not one this page can settle.
limits.classification: Sector is shown as it is held on the organisation's own record, using {classification}. Which classification is used, and what the size bands measure, are open decisions; the values here are demonstration values.

howItWorks.title: How it works
howItWorks.metaDescription: The seven steps from a documented wetland project to issued units: who acts at each step, what evidence exists by then, and what this platform does and does not do.
howItWorks.lead: This page describes what happens between a documented restoration project and units a buyer can retire: who acts at each step, what evidence exists by then, and where this platform's role stops.

flow.title: The seven steps in detail
flow.lead: The same seven steps as on the front page, with the detail a reviewer asks for. For the pilot projects the first two steps are in place: the project idea notes and design documents exist. Verification and issuance come later.
flow.doesNot: What the platform does not do

project.who: The project owner, the organisation that runs the restoration, prepares the project and puts it on the platform. Sylva confirms the records and publishes the page.
project.evidence: A project idea note, and for the pilot projects a project design document. The project boundary as GeoJSON, downloadable from the project page.
project.does: Gives the project its own page at its own URL, so it can be sent to a colleague and read without an account.
project.doesNot: It does not design the project, carry out the works, or judge whether the restoration plan is sound. The project owner is responsible for the project and answers questions about it.

evidence.who: The project owner supplies the figures and the documents behind them. Sylva checks that every figure on the page states where it came from and when.
evidence.evidence: Baselines, the monitoring plan, the named verifier and the stated uncertainty. Claim rights: who may claim each benefit, for what, and what is excluded. Durability: who controls the land, who maintains it, for how long. Availability per period.
evidence.does: Prints the source and the date beside every figure, and says so where the documents are silent.
evidence.doesNot: It does not verify the ecological result. Nothing on the project page at this stage is a verified outcome, and expected figures are labelled as expected.

interest.who: A buyer from an organisation Sylva has approved presses Express interest on the project page.
interest.evidence: An interest event in the permanent record: the project, the buyer, the date. On the public record the buyer appears as a label such as "Buyer 014" with its sector, country and size, unless it has chosen to be named for that deal.
interest.does: Opens a private room between that buyer and that project, and writes the event to the record.
interest.doesNot: It sets no volume, no price and no term. Interest is the first stage marker; the letter of intent and the term sheet come later.

deal.who: The buyer and the project owner, in the private room. Questions go to the project owner and to Sylva, not to a public comment feed.
deal.evidence: Messages, documents, successive versions of the draft terms, and a stage marker running from interest, through a letter of intent and a term sheet, to signed. The signed agreement is uploaded.
deal.does: Keeps every version and writes each stage to the permanent record. Nothing in that record is edited or deleted: a mistake is corrected by a new entry that points at the wrong one, and the wrong one stays visible.
deal.doesNot: It handles no payments, no escrow and no settlement, and it is not where the agreement is signed. Signature happens outside the platform and the signed document is uploaded as evidence.

restoration.who: The project owner and the partners on the ground: whoever develops the project, owns the land, and has committed to maintain it.
restoration.evidence: Monitoring against the plan, and the durability arrangements for the site after the contract ends.
restoration.does: Publishes monitoring documents as they are supplied and keeps earlier versions readable rather than replacing them.
restoration.doesNot: It does not carry out or supervise the works, and it does not monitor the site.

verified.who: An independent verification body, named on the project page before anyone commits.
verified.evidence: A verification report. Until one exists, every outcome on the page is an expectation rather than a result.
verified.does: Publishes the report alongside the documents it tests.
verified.doesNot: It verifies nothing itself and does not decide whether a result meets the scheme's criteria. Sylva is not the verifier.

units.who: The credit scheme issues units under its own rules and records them in its own registry.
units.evidence: The scheme's registry record, and a reference to it held here against this project and this period.
units.does: Records the registry reference, the allocation against commitments made here, and retirement, meaning units taken out of circulation so nobody else can claim the result. No unit is allocated, transferred or retired here without a reference to the scheme's record.
units.doesNot: It issues no units and it is not the registry. A unit exists because the scheme issued it, not because it appears on this platform.

vetting.title: Who can transact
vetting.body: Nobody reaches the private side without being vetted by Sylva first. We ask what the buyer intends to claim, how it operates and what its approach to sustainability is, then approve or decline. This is a condition of our funding and our main safeguard against greenwashing.
vetting.approval: No deal can be created for an organisation we have not approved. Project pages are public and can be read without an account; expressing interest cannot.
vetting.pseudonym: Participation is pseudonymous by default. On the public record a buyer appears as a label with its sector, country and size, and being named is the buyer's own choice, deal by deal.

dealShapes.title: The three deal shapes
dealShapes.lead: All three are offered side by side on every project, because the buyers we interviewed differ on which one they want.
dealShapes.caption: The three deal shapes, as offered on every project.
dealShapes.colRecord: What is recorded on this platform
dealShapes.why: Most deals in this pilot are forward commitments. Units are issued only after an independent body has verified the result on the ground, so at the point where a buyer and a project agree, there is usually nothing in inventory to sell. The platform is built for deals on units that will exist later, not only for deals on units that exist now.

spot.name: Spot volume
spot.commitment: Takes a volume of units that already exist and retires them when ready.
spot.unitsExist: Yes. Already issued by the scheme, with a registry record to reference.
spot.record: The allocation against that registry reference, and the retirement when it happens.

forward.name: Forward contract
forward.commitment: Commits now to take a volume in a future year, on terms agreed now.
forward.unitsExist: No. They are issued only after an independent body has verified the result.
forward.record: The commitment against this project and this period, the successive drafts, and the signed agreement.

coInvestment.name: Co-investment
coInvestment.commitment: Funds a share of the project directly. The volume the company does not need is sold to other buyers.
coInvestment.unitsExist: No. As with a forward contract, issuance follows verification.
coInvestment.record: The agreement, and the volume reserved for the investing company against this project and this period.

units.title: Units, and why two projects' figures are never added
units.lead: The market is new and small. There is no single standard, and different schemes measure different things. One project may sell hectares under restoration for a year; another may sell points on a condition index. Adding those figures produces a number that means nothing.
units.rule: So no screen, export or chart on this platform adds unit volumes across different projects, and every figure is printed with the unit it is measured in. The two blocks below are demonstration data and show why they are kept apart.
units.metricIndexPoints: points on the scheme's condition index
units.tableCaption: Unit figures for {project}: one project, one period, one unit type. Demonstration data.
units.noTotal: There is no combined figure beneath these two blocks, and there will not be one. Hectare-years and index points measure different things, and their sum would describe nothing.

boundaries.title: What this platform is not
boundaries.lead: Five limits, stated plainly, because each one is easy to assume the other way round.

registry.title: It is not the credit registry
registry.body: Each credit scheme runs its own official database of issued and retired units, and gives outside systems no write access to it. This platform holds references to those records together with the supporting documents. Our own record is evidence of what was agreed here; whether a unit exists, and what state it is in, is answered by the scheme's registry and not by us.

payments.title: There are no payments, escrow or settlement
payments.body: No money moves through this platform and we are not building that. Agreements are signed outside the platform, and the signed document is uploaded as evidence of what was agreed.

verifier.title: Sylva is not the verifier
verifier.body: The ecological result is verified by an independent body, named on the project page. We publish what that body reports. Ecological verification and financial performance are two separate questions, and neither answers the other.

evidencePack.title: The reporting evidence pack is not an audit opinion
evidencePack.body: The pack assembles what the platform holds for a project: the measurable action, the timeframe, the expected impact, a budget where one is available, the verification information and the supporting documents. It describes the information available here. It does not guarantee acceptance by any particular auditor.

ownership.title: A unit is not a share of the land
ownership.body: Units are the packaged result of restoration, not an interest in the site. Who controls the land, who maintains it and for how long is set out in each project's long-term protection section.

terms.title: Terms used on this page
terms.lead: This market uses the same words in different ways. These are the meanings used here.

projectOwner.def: The organisation that runs the restoration. It puts the project on the platform and answers questions about it.

buyer.def: A company that takes units and retires them. Two kinds read the same project page differently: one is paying for water in the catchments around its own sites, the other for documentation its reporting will rest on.

investor.def: A fund or bank that finances a project and is repaid from unit sales and other revenue. Financial information is available to investors Sylva has vetted.

coInvestor.def: A company that funds a share of a project directly, keeps the volume it needs, and lets the rest be sold to other buyers.

verifier.def: The independent body that verifies the ecological result. Named on the project page.

scheme.def: The standard a project is registered under. It defines what a unit measures, issues units, and runs its own registry.

unit.def: The packaged result of restoration under a scheme's rules: issued after verification, bought, and then retired.

retirement.def: Taking a unit out of circulation so that nobody else can claim it.

buffer.def: A margin of units held back from sale in case a project delivers less than expected.

catchment.def: The area of land that drains into a particular river or aquifer. A water-dependent buyer usually wants a project in the same catchment as its own sites.

period.def: The year a project's units relate to. The scheme decides whether that means the year of the ecological outcome or the year of issuance, and the project page states which.

dealRoom.def: The private room opened when a buyer expresses interest: messages, documents, draft terms and a stage marker, visible to that buyer and that project only.

forInvestors.title: For investors
forInvestors.lead: Investors finance restoration work and are repaid from sales of units and other project revenue. This page states what financial information a project holds, who can read it, and how to ask for access.

gate.title: Financial information is visible only to investors we have vetted.
gate.body: Financing need, revenue streams and the financial model are released to an investor organisation after Sylva has approved it. The project description, the outcomes, the claim rights, the documents and the availability figures are public and can be read first.

sequence.title: Where an investor enters
sequence.intro: The order below is the usual one for the pilot projects. Each project states which stage it has reached.

documented.name: Project documented
documented.note: The project owner publishes the project idea note and the design document, what will be measured, the monitoring plan and the verifier.

committed.name: Buyers commit
committed.note: Vetted buyers express interest and commit to take a volume of the units the project expects to issue in a future period.

financing.name: Financing discussed
financing.note: Vetted investors read the financing need, the revenue streams and the financial model, and discuss terms with the project owner in a private room.

signed.name: Agreement signed
signed.note: Agreements are signed outside the platform. The signed document is uploaded as evidence and the step is written to the permanent record.

entryCallout.title: Buyers commit before financing is discussed
entryCallout.body: Units are issued only after an independent body has verified the result on the ground, so most agreements here are commitments to future units rather than sales of existing stock. Investors typically come in once buyers have committed volume. A project can be read in full before that point, and the table below states which projects have reached it.

vetting.body1: Sylva vets every organisation before it can transact on the platform. Approval is a condition of the funding under which this pilot runs, and it is our main safeguard against greenwashing.
vetting.body2: No deal can be created for an organisation Sylva has not approved, and a project's financial information stays closed until the organisation asking for it has been approved.
vetting.body3: On the public record a buyer appears as a label such as “Buyer 014” with its sector, country and size, unless that buyer has chosen to be named for that deal. Real names are available to auditors, whose access is read-only.

limits.title: What this page does not contain
limits.returns: No return figures, no yield and no financial projections. None are published on this page, on any project page, or anywhere else on the platform.
limits.noRanking: No ranking and no recommendation. Sylva publishes the information each project owner has documented, together with the verification information the project holds, and does not score projects against one another.
limits.registry: Each credit scheme keeps its own official registry of issued and retired units. This platform is not that registry and does not replace it. It holds references to registry records, the supporting documents, and a permanent record of what was agreed here.
limits.settlement: No payments, no escrow and no settlement. Agreements are signed outside the platform and the signed document is uploaded as evidence.
limits.demo: No real project. Every organisation, project and figure on this page is fictional demonstration data and describes no real wetland, no real verification and no real environmental result.

forBuyers.title: For buyers
forBuyers.metaDescription: What a corporate buyer can do on this platform: review projects, register its own sites to see distances, express interest, complete vetting and negotiate privately.
forBuyers.lead: Two kinds of company buy restoration outcomes, for different reasons, and they read the same project page in a different order. This page sets out both situations, what a buyer can do here, how your identity appears in public, and what we ask before a deal can exist.

situations.title: Two buyer situations
situations.lead: Both situations were described by the organisations interviewed for the pilot. A project page serves both; what differs is which section is read first.

water.heading: The water-dependent buyer
water.who: A power station, a drinks producer, a food manufacturer. Its operations depend on water in a particular river or aquifer, so it wants a project in the catchment its own sites draw from, not simply a project in Europe.
water.ranks: Water outcomes first, biodiversity second. It would claim the biodiversity benefit as well, but water is what it is paying for.
water.read1: The catchment map, and the distance from its own registered sites to the project boundary.
water.read2: The water indicators: what is measured, the baseline, the monitoring method and the stated uncertainty.
water.read3: Claim rights, to check that an onward sale of units cannot remove its right to claim the benefit it paid for.
water.read4: Long-term protection: who controls the land once the contract ends, and who has committed to maintain it.
water.note: European origin as such did not matter to the companies interviewed. The catchment did.

reporting.heading: The reporting-driven buyer
reporting.who: A large company with sustainability reporting obligations. It wants projects near its own assets, and documentation that the person assessing its report will accept.
reporting.ranks: Documentation first: what action was taken, over what period, with what expected impact, at what cost, verified by whom.
reporting.read1: The reporting evidence pack: project description, the measurable action, the timeframe, the expected impact, the budget where available, verification information and the supporting documents.
reporting.read2: The documents themselves: project idea note, project design document, monitoring plan and, once they exist, verification reports, each with its version and date.
reporting.read3: The partners on the ground, including the independent body that verifies the result.
reporting.read4: Availability per period, so a commitment can be dated in its own reporting.
reporting.note: One company told us its assessor asked it to consider projects with a measurable action, a fixed timeframe, an expected impact, a budget and a verification standard. The platform assembles that information and states where each figure comes from. It makes no claim that the pack satisfies any particular auditor, assessment or regulation; that judgement stays with your assessor.

actions.title: What you can do here
actions.lead: Five steps, in the order they happen. A deal cannot exist before your organisation has been approved, and the private room opens only once interest has been expressed.

review.title: Review projects
review.body: Every project has its own page at its own address, so it can be sent to a colleague. The page states the scheme, the unit type, what is measured, who verifies it, who may claim the result, and what remains available in each period.

sites.title: Register your own sites
sites.body: Add your sites with their coordinates once, from your organisation's area after you sign in. Each project page then shows the distance from your sites to that project. The register stays private to your organisation.

interest.title: Express interest
interest.body: One button on the project page records that your organisation is interested and opens a private room with that project. The event goes onto the permanent record; what you then discuss does not.

vetting.title: Be vetted
vetting.body: Sylva reviews every organisation that wants to transact. We ask what you intend to claim, how you operate and how you approach sustainability, then approve or decline. No deal exists on this platform for an organisation we have not approved.

negotiate.title: Negotiate privately
negotiate.body: In the private room: messages, documents, successive versions of the draft terms, and a stage marker running from first interest through a letter of intent and a term sheet to signed. No other buyer sees your terms.

actions.outside: Agreements are signed outside the platform and the signed document is uploaded as evidence. The platform carries no payment, escrow or settlement.

disclosure.lead: Participation is pseudonymous by default. On the public record your organisation appears as a label with its sector, country and size. Being named is your choice, and you make that choice separately for each deal.
disclosure.defaultBody: Nothing on the public record identifies your organisation. A reader sees a buyer label, a sector, a country and a size band, which is enough to follow the project's history without naming you.
disclosure.namedBody: If you flag a deal for disclosure, the public entries for that deal carry your organisation's name. Your other deals are unaffected, and entries already written stay as they were written.

disclosure.appendOnly: The record is append-only. An entry is never edited or deleted; a mistake is corrected by a new entry that points at the wrong one, and the wrong one stays visible.

dealShapes.title: What you can agree
dealShapes.lead: Three shapes, offered side by side on each project, because the buyers interviewed differ on which they want. Most deals in this pilot will be forward contracts: units are issued only after an independent body has verified the result, so there is usually nothing in inventory to sell.
dealShapes.caption: Deal shapes a buyer can agree with a project.

spot.name: Spot volume
spot.what: Units that already exist. You take an agreed volume and retire it when you are ready.
spot.fits: Rare in this pilot, because it needs units that have already been issued.

forward.name: Forward contract
forward.what: You commit now to take a volume in a future period, on terms agreed now.
forward.fits: The usual shape here, and the shape most pilot deals will take.

coinvestment.name: Co-investment
coinvestment.what: You fund a share of the project directly. The volume you do not need is sold to other buyers.
coinvestment.fits: When you want the project to go ahead and do not need all of its volume.

dealShapes.retireBody: Retiring means taking a unit out of circulation so that nobody else can claim it. Retirement is recorded in the credit scheme's own registry. This platform holds the reference to that record; it is not the registry.
dealShapes.landBody: Buying units gives you no interest in the land; the land stays with its owner, whom the project page names. Nor is it a stake in the project's financial performance.

meta.title: About Sylva
meta.description: Who operates this platform, what the EU-funded pilot is for, how organisations are vetted, and how personal data, hosting and analytics are handled.

about.title: About Sylva
about.lead: Sylva operates this platform as part of an EU-funded pilot. This page states who we are, what the pilot is meant to find out, what we check before an organisation can transact here, what this platform does not do, and how personal data is handled.

operator.title: Who operates the platform
operator.lead: Sylva operates this platform. We publish the projects, vet the organisations that want to transact on them, confirm the records shown here, and keep the record of what was agreed.

duty.publishBody: A project owner submits a project. We review what has been submitted and publish the project page.
duty.vetBody: Every organisation that wants to take part in a deal is vetted by us before it can do so.
duty.confirmBody: We confirm the records that appear on a project page and in the public transaction record.
duty.evidenceBody: Agreements are signed outside the platform. The signed document is uploaded here afterwards and held as evidence of what was agreed.
duty.questionsBody: A question asked about a project goes to the project owner and to us. There is no public comment feed.

pilot.title: What the pilot is for
pilot.lead: The pilot tests one question: can a restoration project be presented in enough depth that a large company or an investor can judge it, get in touch privately and agree terms — and can every step of that be recorded so that someone else can follow it afterwards?
pilot.marketTitle: Why the presentation has to be this careful
pilot.marketBody: This market is new and small. There is no single standard, and different schemes measure different things: one project may sell hectares under restoration for a year, another points on an index. Units from two projects are therefore not interchangeable, and nothing on this platform adds them together.
pilot.issuanceBody: Units are issued only after an independent body has verified the result on the ground. Most of what is agreed here is therefore a commitment to units that will exist later, not a sale of something already in stock.
pilot.researchTitle: What the design is based on
pilot.researchLead: Eight organisations were interviewed between June and September 2026, and what they asked for shaped the project page: location and catchment first; water outcomes ahead of biodiversity for the water-dependent buyers; claim rights that survive an onward sale; and participation that stays anonymous unless the buyer chooses otherwise, deal by deal.

roles.lead: Five kinds of organisation use this platform, and they do not see the same thing.
roles.caption: Roles on the platform, and what each one can see
roles.ownerDoes: Run the restoration. Put a project on the platform and answer questions about it.
roles.ownerSees: Their own projects, and the questions asked about them.
roles.buyerDoes: Large companies. Review projects, register their own sites, express interest and agree a volume.
roles.buyerSees: Published projects, and their own sites, questions and deals. Never another buyer's terms.
roles.investorDoes: Funds and banks. Finance a project and are repaid from credit sales and other revenue.
roles.investorSees: Published projects, and the financing information on them once we have vetted them as investors.
roles.operatorDoes: Vet the organisations, confirm the records, publish the projects.
roles.operatorSees: What is needed to do that.
roles.auditorDoes: Read only. Follow the history of a project and of a transaction. Nothing is edited.
roles.auditorSees: The record, the documents and the registry references, for the funder and for external auditors.
roles.note: One buyer seeing another buyer's terms is the failure this platform is most concerned with. What each role may read is decided in the database, table by table, and not in the screens.

limits.title: What this platform does not do
limits.lead: Each of the following would be a costly misreading, so it is stated here rather than left to be inferred.
limits.registry: This is not the credit registry
limits.registryBody: Each credit scheme runs its own official database of issued and retired units, and does not give outside systems write access to it. We hold references to those records and the supporting documents. Our record is evidence of what was agreed here, not the authoritative record of what exists.
limits.issue: We do not issue or verify units
limits.issueBody: An independent body verifies the result on the ground. The scheme issues the units, under its own rules.
limits.moneyBody: There is no payment, escrow or settlement on this platform.
limits.signBody: Agreements are signed outside the platform. The signed document is uploaded here afterwards as evidence.
limits.land: Agreeing a volume is not buying the site
limits.landBody: Who owns the land and who controls it is stated separately on each project page, in the section on long-term protection. Nothing on this platform transfers land.
limits.totals: We do not add units across projects
limits.totalsBody: One project may sell hectares under restoration for a year, another points on an index. No screen, export or chart here totals volumes across projects, and every figure is printed with the unit it is counted in.
limits.auditor: We do not say that a project satisfies an auditor
limits.auditorBody: Each project offers a reporting evidence pack that describes the information available here. It makes no claim that any particular auditor, scheme or regulation will accept it.

vetting.title: Vetting, and what it is for
vetting.lead: No organisation reaches a deal here without being vetted by us first. This is a condition of our funding, and it is our main safeguard against greenwashing.

step.applyBody: It tells us what it intends to claim, how it operates, and its approach to sustainability.
step.decideBody: The decision is ours, and it is recorded.
step.effectBody: An approved organisation can express interest in a project and open a private room with the project owner. No deal can be created for an organisation we have not approved.

vetting.limitBody: Vetting is a judgement we make on the information an organisation gives us. It is not an audit of that organisation, and an approval is not an endorsement of it or of any project.
vetting.claimsBody: One company we interviewed said it would not fund a project if the onward sale of credits took away its right to claim the benefit it had paid for. Another did not want its investment used by someone else as an offset. Every project page therefore states, for each benefit the project produces, who may claim it, what may be claimed and what is excluded.

data.title: Personal data, hosting and analytics
data.lead: Two commitments shape this: personal data is kept in one place so that a person can be removed from it, and loading a page here does not call a third-party service.

fact.regionBody: The application and the database run in a named region in one EU member state — Frankfurt, Paris or Dublin. A generic “Europe” region is not used, because such a region can include locations outside the EU.
fact.personalBody: Personal data is held in one table, the user accounts. Everything else on the platform refers to organisations by an identifier, not to people.
fact.erasureBody: The permanent record holds no reference to a person that would have to be removed along with them, so an account can be deleted without breaking it.
fact.analyticsBody: Usage analytics are self-hosted or hosted in the EU. There are no third-party trackers, no advertising pixels and no cross-site identifiers.
fact.fontsBody: The typeface is served from this platform. A page fetches no font, script or stylesheet from a third-party service, which would otherwise send your IP address to that service on every page view.
fact.identity: Your identity on the public record
fact.identityBody: On the public transaction record a buyer appears as a label such as “Buyer 014”, with its sector, country and size. The organisation's name appears only where that buyer has chosen to be named for that deal.
fact.sitesBody: The sites a buyer registers are visible to that buyer alone. They are used to show the distance from those sites to a project, and another organisation's sites are never shown.
fact.questionsBody: A question asked about a project goes to the project owner and to us. It is not published.

data.erasureTitle: What deleting an account removes, and what it leaves
data.erasureLead: A permanent record and a right to erasure only fit together if the line between them is visible. This is where it falls.

register.lead: Registration has two parts: the organisation that will transact, and the first person who will sign in on its behalf. An account lets you sign in and read published project pages. A deal becomes possible only after Sylva has vetted and approved the organisation.

s1.name: Account created
s1.body: You complete this form. The organisation record and your user account are created together, and you can sign in.
s1.can: Sign in, read published project pages, download project documents and register your own sites.
s1.limit: Expressing interest in a project, or taking part in a deal.

s2.name: Vetting
s2.body: Sylva sends the organisation a questionnaire. It asks what you intend to claim, how you operate and how you approach sustainability. Vetting is a condition of this platform's funding.
s2.can: Complete and return the questionnaire. Carry on reading project pages while it is under review.
s2.limit: Expressing interest in a project, or taking part in a deal.

s3.name: Decision
s3.body: Sylva approves or declines the organisation. No deal can be created for an organisation that has not been approved, so this is the step that opens the private side of the platform.
s3.can: Once approved: express interest in a project and open a private room with that project's owner. Investors approved for financial access can also read financing information.
s3.limit: The account keeps read access to published project pages, and no deal can be created.

vettingForm.title: Vetting questionnaire
vettingForm.metaDescription: The questionnaire an organisation completes before it can take part in a deal: what environmental benefit it intends to claim, where that claim would be published, how it operates, and how it approaches sustainability.
vettingForm.lead: Every organisation that wants to agree a deal on this platform answers these eight questions. We read the answers and then approve or decline. No deal can be created for an organisation we have not approved.
vettingForm.demoNote: Demonstration. This page shows the questionnaire as a signed-in buyer contact would see it. Nothing is saved and nothing is submitted.
vettingForm.whyTitle: Why we ask all of this
vettingForm.whyBody1: Vetting is our main safeguard against greenwashing, and it is a condition of the funding behind this pilot. The questions are about what you intend to claim and how you work, not about your size or your budget.
vettingForm.whyBody2: Every question below states why it is asked. If a question does not apply to your organisation, say so in the answer rather than leaving it empty.
vettingForm.readBy: Your answers are read by Sylva as part of the vetting decision. Auditors for the funder and external auditors have read-only access to platform records.
vettingForm.questionsLead: Five questions in your own words, then three that need a yes or a no. There is no word limit and no right length; an answer we can act on is better than a long one.

org.title: Your organisation
org.statusNote: Your organisation can browse projects and read project evidence now. Expressing interest in a project becomes available once we have approved the organisation.

benefit.label: What environmental benefit do you intend to claim?
benefit.hint: Name the benefit itself - for example a water outcome in a named catchment, or a biodiversity condition result - and the period you would claim it for. If you intend to claim more than one benefit, list each one separately.
benefit.why: Claim rights are set per project and per benefit, and each project states who may claim what and what is excluded. We cannot tell you whether a project's claim rights allow what you have in mind unless you describe it.

publication.label: Where would that claim be published?
publication.hint: For example an annual report, a sustainability statement, a product or packaging label, customer communications, a tender response, or internal reporting only. Name the documents and the audiences.
publication.why: A claim in a public report is read by more people than one kept inside the organisation, and its wording is held to more scrutiny. Where the claim appears is the question our funder asks us about most often, so we ask it before a deal rather than after one.

operations.label: How does your organisation operate?
operations.hint: What you make or do, where your main sites are, and which parts of your activity depend on or affect water, land and habitats. A plain description is enough; no strategy language is needed.
operations.why: We read this answer together with what you intend to claim. A restoration project upstream of your own sites supports a different claim from one with no connection to them, and the project owner needs to know who is asking.

catchments.label: Do you depend on water in specific catchments?
catchments.hint: A catchment is the area of land that drains into a particular river or aquifer. Name the catchments and the sites that depend on them, or state that your activity has no catchment-specific water dependence.
catchments.why: Two of the companies we interviewed want a project in the same catchment as their own sites, and they rank water outcomes ahead of biodiversity. Naming the catchments lets us point you at the projects that sit in them, and tells the project owner which water indicators you will read first. Sites you register stay visible only to you.

sustainability.label: What is your approach to sustainability?
sustainability.hint: How decisions about nature and water are taken in your organisation, who is accountable for them, what you already measure, and what you report. Include work that is under way as well as work that is finished.
sustainability.why: This is the question we weigh most heavily. We are looking at whether a purchase here sits inside a wider approach or stands alone in place of one. An honest answer about work in progress is more useful to us than a polished one.

resale.label: Do you intend to resell units rather than retire them?
resale.hint: Retiring a unit takes it out of circulation so that nobody else can claim the same benefit. Reselling keeps it in circulation for another party.
resale.hintFollowUp: If you intend to resell, describe who you expect to sell to and on what terms. If you intend to retire, say when.
resale.why: Retirement and resale are different products and they lead to different terms. A co-investor may hold more volume than it needs and sell the remainder, which is a normal arrangement here. We ask so that it is agreed openly rather than discovered later.

offset.label: Would you present the benefit as an offset?
offset.hint: An offset framing presents the benefit as compensating for an impact elsewhere.
offset.hintFollowUp: Describe the framing you have in mind and the impact it would be set against.
offset.why: One company we interviewed does not want its investment used by others as an offset. Project owners and other participants take different positions on this, so the framing has to be on the table before terms are drafted. We are asking what you intend; we are not deciding whether such a claim is permitted.

exclusivity.label: Do you require that no other party may claim the same benefit?
exclusivity.hint: That is, whether exclusive claim rights over the benefit you pay for are a condition of your participation.
exclusivity.hintFollowUp: State which benefits exclusivity would need to cover, and for how long.
exclusivity.why: One company told us it would not fund a project if the onward sale of units removed its right to claim the benefit it had paid for, and compared that to signing away the renewable attributes in a power purchase agreement. Exclusivity has to be agreed with the project owner, so we ask whether it is a condition for you before you are matched to a project.

actions.inertNote: This is the frontend build. Neither control saves or submits anything yet.
actions.footNote: You can save a draft and return to it later. Questions you have not answered stay in the list on the left.

next.title: What happens after you submit
next.step1: We read the answers, and we may come back to you with follow-up questions.
next.step2: We approve or decline your organisation, and we tell you which.
next.step3: Once approved, you can express interest in a project. That opens a private room between your organisation and that project owner, and the interest event is written to the permanent record. On the public version of that record your organisation appears as a label such as "Buyer 014" with its sector, country and size, unless you choose to be named for that deal.
next.notBody: Approval is our decision about taking part on this platform. It is not an audit of your organisation, not a verification of what you have told us, and not a statement that a claim you intend to make will be accepted by anyone else.
next.backToBuyers: Read what buyers can do on this platform

demoAnswers.benefit: DEMO ANSWER. We would claim the water outcome - the retention volume and the summer low-flow indicator - for the 2028 period, for the catchment that supplies our Lüneburg bottling site. We would not claim the biodiversity condition result.
demoAnswers.publication: DEMO ANSWER. In our annual sustainability statement, in the water section, and in the environmental annex we give to trade customers on request. Not on packaging and not in advertising.
demoAnswers.operations: DEMO ANSWER. We bottle and distribute mineral water and soft drinks from three sites in northern Germany. Two of the three draw groundwater under abstraction permits. Our exposure is to summer low flow and to falling groundwater levels around the Lüneburg and Uelzen sites.

vettingStatus.gate: No deal can be created on this platform for an organisation Sylva has not approved. Vetting is that approval, and it is a condition of the pilot's funding.

stateMeaning.submitted: The answers have been recorded and are waiting to be read. Nothing further is needed from the organisation at this point.
stateMeaning.under_review: Sylva is reading the application. The organisation can use the public side of the platform in the meantime; it cannot yet express interest in a project.
stateMeaning.approved: The organisation can express interest in a project, which opens a private room between it and that project.
stateMeaning.declined: No deal can be created for the organisation. The public project pages stay open to it.

reason.declinedHeadline: The claim the organisation intended to make could not be reconciled with the claim rights published for the projects it named.
reason.declinedDetail: The application named two projects and described the benefit the organisation intended to claim from them. The claim rights published for both projects assign that benefit to a different holder. Vetting is the point at which Sylva reads what a buyer intends to claim, so the application was declined rather than approved on the assumption that the intended claim would be corrected later.
reason.declinedPart: Part 2 — what the organisation intends to claim

pending.vettingBody: What is collected, who decides, and what approval changes.

declined.projectsBody: A declined decision does not close the public project pages to the organisation.

expressInterest.notAnOffer: This is an enquiry, not an offer, and it does not commit you to buy anything. Terms are discussed privately afterwards, and any agreement is signed outside the platform and uploaded here as evidence.

form.periodsHint: Leave a period blank if you are not interested in it. The volumes are indicative and can change while you talk to the project owner.

form.remainingNote: Remaining is what is left in that period once the buffer the project holds back and the volume already committed or reserved are taken off.
form.dealHint: The three shapes are offered side by side on every project. Choosing one here only tells the project owner where to start.

deal.spotNote: Units that already exist. You take a volume and retire it when you are ready.
deal.forwardNote: You commit now to take a volume in a future period on agreed terms. Most pilot deals take this shape, because units are issued only after an independent body has verified the result.
deal.coInvestmentNote: You fund a share of the project directly, and the volume you do not need is sold to other buyers.
deal.undecidedNote: You want the project owner to walk you through the options first.

confirmation.body: The project owner and Sylva have been notified and will be in touch. Keep the reference below if you need to ask us about this enquiry.

confirmation.publicRecordNamed: You asked to be named for this deal, so the public record shows your organisation's name.
confirmation.volumesCaption: The volumes in this enquiry, per period of this project.
confirmation.noTotalNote: The periods are listed separately and are not added together: a volume in 2028 and a volume in 2029 are different deliverables.
confirmation.next1: The project owner replies to you by email.
confirmation.next2: Sylva sees the same enquiry and can arrange a call with the people running the project.
confirmation.next3: You can send further enquiries about other periods or other projects. Each one is recorded separately.
confirmation.dealRoomBody: The deal room — private messages, drafts of the terms, versions of each document, and a stage marker running from first interest through a letter of intent and a term sheet to signed — opens in a later release. Until then this conversation happens by email.
confirmation.signingBody: Agreements are signed outside the platform in any case, and the signed document is uploaded here as evidence. Sylva does not handle payments or settlement.
confirmation.permanentNote: The interest event is written to the permanent record. Entries there are never edited or deleted: a mistake is corrected by a new entry that points at the wrong one, and the wrong one stays visible.

q214.question: If we commit now, under a forward contract, to a volume for 2028 and later sell part of it on, does the right to claim the water benefit stay with us or move with the units? We would not take part if an onward sale removed the claim we had paid for.
q214.draft: The claim rights section on the project page sets this out benefit by benefit. Before I answer what happens on an onward sale I want the wording of the scheme document in front of me rather than answer from memory, so let me come back to you on that part.

q213.question: Your availability table holds a buffer back from the expected issuance for 2028. Is the buffer released once verification comes in at or above the expected result, or is it held for the whole contract period?
q213.reply: The buffer is held until the verification report for that period has been issued. What happens to an unused buffer after that is set by the scheme rather than by us, and the monitoring plan on the project page names the scheme document and the clause. I would rather point you to it than summarise it here.

q212.question: Two of our bottling sites are in the same catchment. Can you tell us the distance from the project boundary to the site we registered last week, or do we read that off the project page ourselves?

q209.question: The contract period in your design document is five years. Who maintains the site after that, and is that commitment written down somewhere we can read?
q209.reply: The long-term protection section on the project page names the body that has committed to maintain the site and the period it has committed for, and the management agreement itself is in the documents list with its version and date. Nothing after the contract period has been verified yet, so what you can read there is the commitment, not a result.

adminVetting.title: Vetting queue

adminVetting.answersLead: All {count} answers as submitted, in the order they were asked. Nothing is shortened or hidden behind a control.

model.title: How approval is recorded
model.recorded: An operator does not set an organisation's state. It records a decision — approve, decline or suspend — with a reason, as one entry against the application.
model.derived: The state shown here, in the queue above and everywhere else on the platform is read back from those entries. There is no approval field to edit.
model.corrected: A decision recorded in error is corrected by a new entry that points at it. The earlier entry keeps its row and its reason, and the state is read again from the entries that remain.
model.caption: What each recorded entry means for the organisation's state
model.recomputedState: Read again from the remaining entries
model.gate: No deal can be created for an organisation that has not been approved. Approval is therefore the only entry on this list that opens a deal room.
model.openTitle: Not settled by the pilot material
model.openSuspension: What a suspension does to a deal already agreed. The concept note describes approval and decline, and does not say whether an agreed deal continues, pauses or ends. This screen does not state it either.
model.openReason: How much of the recorded reason the applicant reads. The reason is part of the record; whether the organisation is shown it in full has not been settled.

parts.claimNote: Which benefit the buyer intends to claim, and where the claim would appear. These answers are why vetting exists: they are what the decision is mainly read against.
parts.operationsNote: What the organisation does, which catchments it depends on, and how it approaches sustainability.
parts.conditionsNote: Three conditions rather than descriptions, so each is answered with a word. They decide which deal shapes are open to this organisation, and they are read together.

q.benefit: Which benefit does the organisation intend to claim, and for which reporting period?
q.publication: Where would that claim be published?
q.operations: What does the organisation do, and where does it operate?
q.catchments: Which catchments do the organisation's own sites depend on?
q.sustainability: How does the organisation approach sustainability, and who is accountable for it internally?
q.resale: Would units bought here be resold?
q.offset: Would the units be used as an offset against the organisation's own emissions?
q.exclusivity: Does the organisation require exclusive claim rights to the benefit it pays for?

answers.benefit: The water outcome, for the reporting year in which the units are issued. We would report the biodiversity outcome alongside it as context and would not claim it separately. We are not seeking a carbon claim.
answers.publication: In the annual report, in the sustainability statement, and in the catchment section of the water report we publish for our three production sites. Claims would be attributed to the named project and to the scheme that issues the units.
answers.operations: Three beverage bottling sites in northern Germany, around 900 employees in total. All three draw water from the same two catchments. Production is seasonal, with the highest abstraction between May and September.
answers.catchments: The Havel and the lower Elbe. The Rathenow site sits about 14 km from the DEMO Untere Havel project boundary; the other two are further downstream.
answers.sustainability: A water stewardship plan agreed by the management board in 2025 and reviewed annually. It is owned by the operations director, not by communications. Our reporting is assured externally, and the assurer has asked us to show a measurable action with a fixed timeframe, an expected impact, a budget and a verification standard for any project we fund.
answers.resale: No. We would retire the units against our own reporting and would not pass them on. If our need falls, we would rather release the volume back to the project than resell it.
answers.offset: No. We would report the water outcome as a catchment action and would not net it against emissions.
answers.exclusivity: Yes, for the water outcome, for the periods we commit to. We would not fund a project where the same water outcome for the same period could also be claimed by another buyer. We do not ask for exclusivity over the biodiversity outcome.

reason.approvedFund: Investor role. Mandate, fund documentation and the stated approach to claim rights were read and are consistent with the pilot.
reason.approvedOwner: Project owner role. Land control and the named verifier were confirmed against the documents supplied.
reason.approvedKraft: Investor role. Financing need and revenue expectations were read, and no claim over project outcomes was asserted.
reason.suspendedKraft: Suspended at the organisation's own request while it reorganises its European holdings. To be read again when it asks.
reason.declinedLogistics: The organisation asked for exclusive claim rights over every outcome of a project it would part-fund, including outcomes it does not pay for, and would publish the claim as an offset against its own emissions. Both are outside what the pilot offers.

log.readsAsNote: Read from the entries above, in order. Nothing else sets it.

example.title: How a decision recorded in error is corrected
example.body: A worked example, from an application decided before this extract. Nothing is edited and nothing is deleted: a correction is one more entry, and the entry it corrects stays on screen.
example.step1: An approval was recorded as entry {wrong}, with its reason.
example.step2: A later entry, {correction}, points at {wrong} and carries its own reason. {wrong} keeps its row and gains the word Corrected.
example.step3: The state of application {application} is then read again from the entries that remain. What was recorded first, and why it changed, both stay readable.
example.close: This is the append-only record the concept note requires: a mistake is corrected by a new entry that points at the wrong one, and the wrong one stays visible.

decide.title: Record a decision
decide.lead: One entry against {organisation}, with a reason. Recording it does not change a stored state; the state is read again from the entries afterwards.
decide.unsettled: Effect on an agreed deal not settled
decide.reasonHelp: Write for two readers: the applicant, and whoever reads this record in five years. Say what in the answers above the decision turns on.
decide.reasonPart: The reason is stored with the entry and cannot be edited afterwards. A correction is a new entry that points at this one and carries its own reason.
decide.inertNote: This is a frontend pass. The control below is inert: no entry is written, no state changes, and nothing is sent to the organisation.
decide.notAFlag: Recording this entry does not set an approval flag. There is no such field. The organisation's state is read again from its entries, this one included.
decide.appendOnly: Nothing on this screen edits or deletes an earlier entry.
decide.noReasonNoEntry: A decision cannot be recorded without a reason. An entry that cannot later be edited to explain itself would be permanently unexplained.

decision.declineNote: No deal. The organisation is told the recorded reason.
decision.suspendNote: No new interest is expressed while the suspension stands. Use it when an approved organisation should not proceed for now, and say why in the reason.

section.interestsIntro: Every interest your organisation has expressed, newest first. A closed entry stays in the list, because the record is append-only.

section.documentsIntro: Documents your organisation has lodged or received, grouped by what they belong to. A superseded version stays in the list.
section.dealsIntro: One card per deal. Each volume belongs to one project, one period and one unit type, and volumes on different cards are not comparable.
